title: "chisquare"
format: docx

A **chi-square test of independence** was run to examine whether **Relation type** and **Explicitation status** are statistically associated.

> Are explicitations distributed similarly across Contrast and Consequence relations, or is there a statistically meaningful difference?

```{r}
data <- matrix(c(48, 732,
                 102, 497),
               nrow = 2,
               byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(
                 Relation = c("Contrast", "Consequence"),
                 Explicitation = c("Explicit", "NonExplicit")
               ))

```

```{r}
# 查看表格
print(data)
```

```{r}
# 执行卡方独立性检验（关闭连续性校正）
result <- chisq.test(data,correct = FALSE)

# 输出结果
print(result)
```

Expected counts represent what we would expect **if Relation and Explicitation were independent**.

For example, under independence, the test expected about **84.84 Explicit cases** in the Contrast row, but you observed only **48**. That is much lower than expected.

Likewise, the test expected about **65.16 Explicit cases** in the Consequence row, but you observed **102**. That is much higher than expected.

All expected counts are well above 5, so the chi-square approximation is appropriate.

```{r}
result$expected
```

Standardized residuals show which cells contribute most strongly to the significant result.

A rough rule of thumb is:

| Residual size       | Interpretation        |
|---------------------|-----------------------|
| around ±2           | notable deviation     |
| around ±3 or larger | strong deviation      |
| ±6.429              | very strong deviation |

So, the significant chi-square result is driven by the fact that **Consequence relations are much more likely to be Explicit**, while **Contrast relations are much more likely to be NonExplicit**.

```{r}
# 事后分析：标准化残差（standardized residuals）
std_res <- result$stdres
print(round(std_res, 3))
```

> A Pearson chi-square test of independence was conducted to examine the relationship between Relation type and Explicitation status. The association was statistically significant, χ²(1, N = 1379) = 41.33, p \< .001, Cramér’s V = .173. Consequence relations were more likely to be explicit than Contrast relations: 17.03% of Consequence relations were Explicit, compared with 6.15% of Contrast relations. Standardized residuals showed that Explicit cases were underrepresented among Contrast relations and overrepresented among Consequence relations, with residuals of ±6.429.
